body: {"total":2,"records":[{"title":"Group antenatal care and attendance at recommended contacts: a cluster randomised trial in 24 community clinics","authors":"Adjei-Lindholm M, Carrasco-Whyte E, Okwuosa-Brandt L","year":2022,"venue":"Midwifery Trials Journal","doi":"10.5555/mtj.2022.0174","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 24 community clinics to offer group antenatal care or individual appointments to women booking before 16 weeks of pregnancy. Among 2,960 women, 71 percent in group-care clinics and 58 percent in individual-care clinics attended eight or more contacts (risk ratio 1.22, 95 percent confidence interval 1.09 to 1.37). The difference was larger among women under 20. Only 46 percent of women offered group care took it up. Preterm birth and low birthweight did not differ between arms. Costs were not measured, and clinics in the most deprived areas were under-represented."},{"title":"Costs of group versus individual antenatal care: a micro-costing study in two maternity services","authors":"Haverford-Nakamura T, Obi-Castellanos R","year":2016,"venue":"Maternity Services Economics","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We micro-costed antenatal care for 412 women receiving group care and 398 receiving individual care in two maternity services. Midwife time per woman was similar, but group care required room hire, refreshments, childcare and interpreters, so the mean cost per woman was 12 percent higher (mean difference 64 in local currency). Costs per woman fell as group size rose from 8 to 12. The study did not measure attendance or outcomes, so cost-effectiveness could not be estimated. Interpreter costs varied most between the two services."}]}
